name: SAPHO syndrome
aliases: synovitis acne pustulosis hyperostosis osteitis syndrome
chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis with skin involvement

clinicalPearls: Defined by the pentad of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis and osteitis, though few patients show all features simultaneously
The anterior chest wall (sternoclavicular and sternocostoclavicular region) is the most characteristic site, producing painful bony swelling and hyperostosis
Palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne (including acne fulminans and conglobata) are the typical dermatological associations, but skin disease may precede, follow or never accompany the bone disease
Regarded as part of the autoinflammatory spectrum and overlapping closely with chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis in children
Bone lesions are sterile; cultures are negative and the disorder is not a true pyogenic infection
Bone scintigraphy classically shows the 'bull's head' sign of tracer uptake across the manubrium and both sternoclavicular joints
Management uses NSAIDs first-line, with bisphosphonates, conventional and biologic DMARDs (including TNF and IL-1 directed therapy) for refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: SAPHO syndrome is considered a sterile autoinflammatory disorder in which innate immune dysregulation drives neutrophil-rich inflammation of bone, joints and skin. Aberrant activation of the innate immune system, with a role proposed for cutaneous commensal organisms such as Cutibacterium acnes acting as an immune trigger rather than a true infection, promotes release of pro-inflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-17, interleukin-23 and tumour necrosis factor. The result is osteitis with reactive new bone formation (hyperostosis), synovitis at adjacent joints, and neutrophilic skin lesions. It shares genetic and mechanistic features with the paediatric entity chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, and both are viewed as ends of one autoinflammatory sterile osteomyelitis spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Bone metastases or primary bone tumour
additionalInvestigations: Whole-body MRI or technetium bone scintigraphy to map multifocal osteitis and detect the anterior chest wall 'bull's head' pattern
Plain radiographs and CT of the anterior chest wall showing hyperostosis and sclerosis
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), which are often mildly to moderately raised
Bone biopsy with culture to exclude infection and malignancy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Dermatological assessment for palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne
redFlags: Features suggesting true infective osteomyelitis (fever, rigors, positive cultures, rapidly progressive destruction)
Bony destruction or a mass raising concern for malignancy requiring biopsy
Neurological compromise from spinal involvement or vertebral collapse
Vascular compression at the anterior chest wall (e.g. subclavian vein thrombosis)
reference.prognosis: SAPHO syndrome typically follows a chronic relapsing-remitting course; most patients maintain function, but persistent anterior chest wall hyperostosis, spinal involvement and cutaneous flares can cause long-term pain and disability.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing sterile osteitis as pyogenic osteomyelitis and giving prolonged unnecessary antibiotics or surgery
Overlooking the diagnosis when skin disease is absent or separated in time from bone symptoms
Attributing anterior chest wall pain to cardiac disease and missing the characteristic bone lesions
Failing to recognise the overlap with paediatric chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis
